topics: Intro and objectives; Product overview (API + Console); Live demo of chat/text generation (streaming, params); SDK code paths and retries; Observability and cost breakdown in Console; Security/Compliance (SOC2, SSO, KMS, audit logs); POC conversation and next steps.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, um we're gonna keep this to about 30-40 minutes and then leave time for q's. Quick intros?
[00:12] Asha Rao: Asha Rao, CTO at Skyline, thanks for organizing.
[00:16] Ben Miller: Ben here, Lead ML Eng. I'll be the hands-on for the POC.
[00:20] Tom Alvarez: Tom, DevOps, I'll handle networking/security.
[00:25] Maya Chen: Great thanks. Ravi and Jules from my side will cover the tech demo and console.
[00:30] Ravi Patel: Hi all. Quick agenda: hosted API basics, streaming, params, retries, then console observability and cost.
[00:42] Jules Nguyen: We'll show a couple of example payloads and how to tune for cost vs latency.
[00:48] Maya Chen: Customer goal?
[00:50] Asha Rao: We want to add an assistant in our product that can answer docs and perform simple tasks. Need low p99 latency and reasonable cost. Considering hosted to start but Dedicated or private could be needed for data residency.
[01:05] Ben Miller: Our typical prompt sizes are 200-800 tokens and we do a lot of short queries too, 1-3 sentences. Peak RPS expected around 150-200 for the initial rollout.
[01:18] Tom Alvarez: We need SOC2, SSO, and ability to bring our own KMS. Network peering is a must.
[01:25] Maya Chen: Perfect, that's helpful. I'll hand off to Ravi for the demo.
[01:30] Ravi Patel: Alright jumping into the hosted API. First, the simple call is a POST to /v1/chat with a model param. We support streaming where tokens arrive incrementally over an SSE or chunked response. Streaming reduces time-to-first-byte and helps perceived latency.
[01:52] Ben Miller: Is streaming compatible with function calling?
[01:55] Ravi Patel: Yes, we support streaming plus function/tool calling together, though tool calls may change the shape of the stream a bit.
[02:03] Ravi Patel: Example params: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop, presence_penalty. For deterministic outputs we set temperature=0 and top_p=1. For creative answers higher temperature.
[02:20] Jules Nguyen: Also mention response trimming and token limits — model-specific.
[02:25] Ben Miller: How do you calculate cost? Is it per token in the prompt + response?
[02:29] Maya Chen: Yes billed per-token; Console shows a token-level breakdown and per-route cost. Our Optimize module can suggest quantization and batching to reduce cost.
[02:40] Ravi Patel: Live demo — I'm going to run two requests: one non-streaming and one streaming so you can see latency differences.
[02:50] [03:00] Ravi Patel: (runs non-streaming) Response took about 420 ms. Now streaming...
[03:15] [03:20] Ravi Patel: Streaming returned first token at ~120 ms and full output at ~380 ms, so you get earlier first byte.
[03:30] Ben Miller: Those numbers are promising at 200 RPS?
[03:34] Ravi Patel: Depends on model and hardware; for hosted we have autoscaling and can hit those RPS numbers with pipelined batching. We also use prefix/kv cache when sessions reuse context which dramatically reduces per-token compute.
[03:53] Tom Alvarez: On networking, how do you handle VPC or private peering?
[03:57] Jules Nguyen: For hosted we offer VPC peering and private endpoints; for stricter requirements we have Dedicated or Private deployments with customer-managed VPC.
[04:12] Asha Rao: Is there any variance in p99 with streaming enabled?
[04:15] Ravi Patel: Streaming generally improves time-to-first-byte; p99 end-to-end may still be influenced by batching policies and load. We can tune batching window to trade latency for throughput.
[04:30] Ben Miller: Can you show SDK use?
[04:33] Ravi Patel: Sure. Sample code in node/python — you set up a client, call client.chat.create(...). Retries are built in with exponential backoff by default and a jitter factor. We also expose hooks to intercept retry events and log them for observability.
[04:55] [05:00] Ravi Patel: Note: if you get 429 or transient 5xx, the SDK retries with increasing delays up to a configurable max. You can also elect to do idempotency tokens for certain request types.
[05:15] Ben Miller: What's the default retry count?
[05:18] Ravi Patel: Default is 3 with exponential backoff; we recommend keeping it small for latency-sensitive paths but you can tune per-route.
[05:26] Tom Alvarez: Do retries double-bill?
[05:29] Maya Chen: If the request completes twice due to a client retry that reached past our timeout then yes you could be billed for two responses; SDKs try to avoid that with idempotency/ack patterns. We also provide server-side request IDs to reconcile.
[05:45] Asha Rao: Security — SOC2, SSO and KMS?
[05:49] Jules Nguyen: Redwood is SOC2 compliant, supports SAML/SSO, RBAC, and integrates with KMS/HSM for key management. We persist audit logs and can ship them to your SIEM.
[06:05] Tom Alvarez: For KMS, do you allow BYOK and HSM-backed keys?
[06:09] Jules Nguyen: Yes BYOK and HSM are supported in Dedicated and Private; hosted supports customer-managed keys via a delegated KMS integration.
[06:20] Ben Miller: What about data retention and logs? We need 90-day logs for audit.
[06:25] Maya Chen: Console has configurable retention tiers; we can keep detailed logs for 90+ days on enterprise add-on.
[06:32] Ravi Patel: Back to streaming: one common gotcha is SSE proxies in some infra that buffer chunked transfers; we document workaround headers and recommend config for mobile clients.
[06:48] Ben Miller: Can we set token limits per user/session?
[06:52] Ravi Patel: You can enforce max_tokens and application-side limits. Console also supports per-route quotas.
[07:00] Asha Rao: About fallbacks — if capacity is constrained do you have automatic fallback to smaller models?
[07:06] Maya Chen: Yes, smart routing can fall back to cheaper model variants or alternate regions based on policy; we surface those in the console and via routing rules.
[07:18] Tom Alvarez: Would that break prompt compatibility?
[07:20] Ravi Patel: There can be behavioral differences; we recommend canary rollouts and evals before automatic fallback for critical flows.
[07:28] Ben Miller: Can you show the Console cost/latency dashboard?
[07:31] Jules Nguyen: (shares screen) Here is the per-route token usage, p50/p90/p99 latencies, and token cost. You can drill into a route and see sample request traces and tokens per request.
[07:48] [08:00] Jules Nguyen: We also have an Optimize tab which gives batching and quantization suggestions based on your traffic profile. For example it recommended batching window 20ms for one of our retail customers to lower unit cost.
[08:18] Ben Miller: Is quantization available for hosted models?
[08:22] Ravi Patel: We host both full precision and quantized variants; the model catalog shows verified perf/quality tradeoffs. Optimize can recommend when to use a quantized variant.
[08:33] Asha Rao: For our docs assistant, we need consistent quality; quantization is risky.
[08:36] Maya Chen: Totally understood—Optimize ties suggestions to evals and prompt sets so you can detect regressions in quality.
[08:46] Ben Miller: Regarding throughput — you mentioned KV cache earlier. Can you explain how that works for chat sessions?
[08:52] Ravi Patel: KV cache stores decoder-side key/value pairs for recently used contexts so when you append more tokens you don't recompute earlier layers; it's especially useful with long histories or reused prefixes. Hosted supports per-session KV caching with eviction policies.
[09:10] Tom Alvarez: That sounds good. How about monitoring for model regressions?
[09:14] Jules Nguyen: We integrate evals and can run continuous checks on a prompt set; alerts trigger regressions if generated outputs drop below thresholds.
[09:23] Ben Miller: Any built-in A/B or canary for model rollouts?
[09:26] Maya Chen: Yes, rollouts in Console let you do canary percentages, A/B tests, and automatic rollback based on defined metrics.
[09:36] Asha Rao: What about onboarding time — if we start hosted how quick to go live?
[09:40] Maya Chen: Most teams get up in hours to days for a simple hosted integration; Dedicated or Private needs capacity planning and lead time.
[09:48] Ben Miller: Could you talk about retries in more detail—how to design the client for idempotency?
[09:53] Ravi Patel: For completion style responses, include a client request id and de-dup logic; for streaming partial responses you can checkpoint the acked position. SDKs have helpers for idempotency tokens and replay protection.
[10:10] Tom Alvarez: What's the recommended approach for sensitive PII in prompts?
[10:13] Jules Nguyen: For PII we recommend redaction/pseudonymization client-side. For enterprise customers we offer data deletion policies and Private deployment to keep data on-prem.
[10:26] Ben Miller: Could you show an example of a streaming chunk and how to handle partial JSON outputs?
[10:30] Ravi Patel: Sure — streaming may send partial tokens; we recommend buffering until a complete JSON object is parsed or using the SDK's streaming parser which handles these cases. (demo)
[10:50] [11:00] Ravi Patel: Quick note: some clients expect newline-delimited JSON; our SDK can normalize to that pattern.
[11:08] Asha Rao: Any known issues with proxies or mobile clients?
[11:11] Ravi Patel: Yep proxies like some CDNs sometimes buffer SSE; mobile networks may coalesce packets. We recommend heartbeat events and chunk flushing headers.
[11:25] Ben Miller: On the billing side, do you provide forecasts?
[11:29] Maya Chen: Console has cost forecast based on actual usage and projected RPS; you can set budget alerts.
[11:36] Tom Alvarez: For network peering, what's latency penalty typical?
[11:40] Jules Nguyen: Minimal if peering is close regionally; cross-region peering adds RTT. We can run a network test during POC to quantify.
[11:52] Ben Miller: For our traffic distribution, a lot of requests are short. Any recommendations to reduce unit cost?
[11:57] Ravi Patel: Use caching for repeated prefixes, consider a smaller/cheaper model for short queries, and tune batching. Optimize can identify the biggest savings.
[12:10] [12:30] Ravi Patel: Now a short QA on SDK features: client-side hooks, retry/backoff, streaming parsing, and telemetry.
[12:45] Ben Miller: Telemetry — can we get traces into our APM?
[12:48] Jules Nguyen: Yes you can export traces to Datadog/NewRelic/Splunk; we also include request IDs for correlation.
[13:00] Asha Rao: Platform SLAs?
[13:03] Maya Chen: Hosted has standard uptime SLAs for paid tiers; Dedicated has SLA-backed latency targets. We can share the SLA doc after.
[13:12] Tom Alvarez: Is there a rate limiting scheme we should be aware of?
[13:15] Ravi Patel: Yes per-API key quotas and per-route limits; rate limit headers are returned and SDK exposes them for backoff decisions.
[13:24] Ben Miller: If we wanted to run a POC, what data would you need from us?
[13:28] Maya Chen: Sample traffic profile, token distribution, target SLOs, a list of sensitive data requirements, and a contact on infra and ML. Ben and Tom are perfect.
[13:40] Asha Rao: We're aiming for a Jan pilot.
[13:43] Maya Chen: Great. We'll send docs and the benchmark sheet.
[13:47] [14:00] Ravi Patel: Quick note on model catalog — it's curated with perf/quality profiles. For each model we surface cost per 1k tokens and p50/p90 latencies.
[14:13] Ben Miller: Do you automatically select kernels or do we need to tune?
[14:17] Ravi Patel: The serving runtime selects optimized kernels then the compile layer picks best kernel based on arch and sequence length; customers don't pick kernels manually.
[14:28] Tom Alvarez: On Dedicated, can we reserve GPU types?
[14:31] Jules Nguyen: Yes, Dedicated lets you reserve GPU pools with predictable throughput and isolation.
[14:38] Ben Miller: Can you share an example of a backoff policy you recommend?
[14:42] Ravi Patel: Exponential backoff with jitter; start with base jitter 200ms, multiplier 2, and cap at 2s for interactive flows. For high-throughput async flows bump caps.
[14:55] Asha Rao: What about model versioning and rollbacks?
[14:58] Maya Chen: Console supports model pinning by route/version and automatic rollback based on evaluation metrics.
[15:05] Ben Miller: How are embeddings billed compared to chat?
[15:09] Ravi Patel: Embeddings billed per embedding unit; pricing differs and Console shows a separate cost area.
[15:18] Tom Alvarez: Are there any compliance docs you can share?
[15:21] Maya Chen: Yes we'll share SOC2, encryption and compliance pack in the follow-up.
[15:28] Ben Miller: One last technical: do you support long context windows e.g., 32k?
[15:33] Ravi Patel: Yes we support models with long context windows; note cost scales with tokens, and kernel selection is optimized for long sequences.
[15:44] Asha Rao: Ok I'm going to hand off to Ben for specifics for the POC.
[15:48] Ben Miller: For the POC we'll test 2 models, streaming vs non-streaming, and run throughput at 100/200 RPS. We'll provide traces and sample prompts.
[15:58] Tom Alvarez: I'll provide network details and peering requirements.
[16:03] Maya Chen: Sounds good — to recap we'll send pricing, benchmark sheet, and SOC2+KMS docs, then schedule the POC scoping.
[16:12] Asha Rao: Thanks everyone. A couple quick Qs — do you have any references in fintech or healthcare?
[16:18] Maya Chen: We have customers in fintech and health on Dedicated/Private; we'll include anonymized case notes.
[16:26] Ben Miller: One operational question — how are model updates scheduled?
[16:29] Jules Nguyen: Updates are deployable via rollouts; we surface changelogs and eval results before you flip traffic.
[16:38] Tom Alvarez: Any cost savings levers during POC?
[16:41] Ravi Patel: Use lower cost variants for synthetic load, and rely on sampling for full-quality runs; Optimize will flag biggest wins.
[16:52] [17:00] Maya Chen: Ok we'll follow up with the docs. Thanks all.
[17:05] Asha Rao: Thanks, helpful session.
[17:08] Ben Miller: Appreciate it.
[17:10] Tom Alvarez: Thanks.
[17:12] Maya Chen: We'll email the materials and set the scoping meeting.
[17:20] [end transcript approximate 00:42:00]
